Computational formulas in cifcurve()

Source: vignettes/v4_formulas.Rmd
v4_formulas.Rmd

How to use this vignette

cifcurve() computes Kaplan–Meier (KM) survival curves and Aalen–Johansen (AJ) cumulative incidence functions (CIFs), along with pointwise standard errors and confidence intervals. This vignette documents how cifcurve() computes its estimates, variances, and intervals. For analysis workflows and publication tables, see Worked examples and Reporting results.

The main arguments control distinct parts of the calculation:

Argument What it controls Options or default
outcome.type Estimated probability "survival" (KM) or "competing-risk" (AJ)
weights Case weights Optional, treated as fixed
error Standard-error calculation Greenwood/Tsiatis (KM); delta/Aalen (AJ); "if" or "fay" (both)
conf.dist CI reference distribution "normal" (default) or "t"
conf.type CI transformation "arcsine-square root" (default), "plain", "log", "log-log", "logit"
df.method Working df for Student CIs "deletion" (FDF, default) or "equal" (EDF, IF-t only)
report.influence.function Return empirical IF contributions FALSE (default)
engine Computation back end "calculateAJ_Rcpp" (default)
n.risk.type Displayed risk-set counts "weighted" (default), "unweighted", or "ess"; estimates unchanged

Here, IF denotes influence function and FG denotes Fay–Graubard (not Fine–Gray regression). FDF denotes Fay-type working degrees of freedom, and EDF denotes equal-allocation working degrees of freedom. FDF and EDF describe working-df allocations, not variance corrections.

With unweighted data, error = NULL selects Greenwood variance for KM and delta-method variance for AJ. When case weights are supplied, the default is error = "if"; the available weighted variance methods are "if" and "fay". Setting conf.dist = "t" without specifying error also selects "if" and computes working degrees of freedom. None of error, conf.dist, conf.type, or df.method changes the point estimate; they affect its uncertainty estimates or confidence limits.

For competing-risk outcomes, fit$surv contains one minus the event-1 CIF, not overall event-free survival. To obtain CIF confidence limits, complement the stored limits and reverse their order. All supplied weights, including externally estimated IPTW, are treated as fixed; uncertainty from propensity-score estimation is not included. The default C++ engine handles tied event times and implements the IF and FG calculations described below.

The sections below cover KM/AJ formulas, the implemented IF and Fay–Graubard calculations, working degrees of freedom, and confidence-interval transformations. Weighted Greenwood/Tsiatis formulas are included for comparison; they are not available as weighted error options in cifcurve().

Kaplan–Meier estimation and classical variances

For outcome.type = "survival", fit$surv contains the KM survival estimate. With unweighted data, error = "greenwood" is the default; error = "tsiatis" selects the alternative classical standard error. Let t1<t2<⋯<tDt_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_D denote the distinct event times, YjY_j the number at risk just before tjt_j, and djd_j the number of events at tjt_j. The KM estimator of S(t)S(t) is

Kaplan–Meier estimator

Ŝ(t)=∏tj≤t(1−djYj) \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{Y_j} \right) The estimator is right-continuous, so events at tjt_j contribute to Ŝ(tj)\hat S(t_j).

For unweighted KM estimates, cifcurve() offers Greenwood and Tsiatis variance formulas (Tsiatis, 1981). The formulas differ in their denominators:

Greenwood variance Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjYj(Yj−dj) \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)}

Tsiatis variance Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjYj2 \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{Y_j^2}

For weighted data, let wiw_i be the supplied case weight, and let djwd_j^w and YjwY_j^w be the weighted event count and risk-set size at tjt_j. The weighted KM estimator is

Ŝ(t)=∏tj≤t(1−djwYjw). \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left( 1 - \frac{d_j^w}{Y_j^w} \right). Xie and Liu (2005) proposed the following adjusted Greenwood expression:

Greenwood variance for weighted Kaplan–Meier Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjwMj(Yjw−djw), \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j^w}{M_j (Y_j^w - d_j^w)}, where MjM_j is an adjustment factor defined as Mj=(∑ti≥tjwi)2∑ti≥tjwi2. M_j = \frac{\left(\sum_{t_i \geq t_j} w_i \right)^2}{\sum_{t_i \geq t_j} w_i^2}. For comparison, the analogous Tsiatis-type expression uses the corresponding first-order denominator. It is not the variance formula proposed by Xie and Liu (2005).

Tsiatis variance for weighted Kaplan–Meier Var{Ŝ(t)}=Ŝ(t)2∑tj≤tdjwMjYjw \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{S}(t)\right \} = \hat{S}(t)^2\sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j^w}{M_j Y_j^w}

Neither weighted formula is selectable through error in the current cifcurve() implementation. With weights, use error = "if" or "fay". Requesting another variance method issues a warning and falls back to IF.

Aalen–Johansen estimation and classical variances

With outcome.type = "competing-risk", cifcurve() estimates the event-1 CIF using AJ. For unweighted data, error = "delta" is the default, while error = "aalen" selects the alternative classical variance. In the formulas, cause 1 is the event of interest, cause 2 is the competing event, djkd_{jk} counts cause-kk events at tjt_j, and dj=dj1+dj2d_j=d_{j1}+d_{j2}. AJ weights each cause-specific event increment by the probability of remaining event-free just before that time.

For cause kk, the estimator is

Aalen-Johansen estimator

F̂k(t)=∑tj≤tdjkYjŜ(tj−1). \hat{F}_k(t) = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_{jk}}{Y_j}\,\hat{S}(t_{j-1}).

Here Ŝ(tj−1)=Ŝ(tj−)\hat S(t_{j-1})=\hat S(t_j-) is overall event-free survival immediately before tjt_j, with Ŝ(t0)=1\hat S(t_0)=1. It differs from the $surv component of a competing-risk fit, which stores 1−F̂1(t)1-\hat F_1(t).

For unweighted AJ estimates, error selects either the Aalen (1978) or delta-method variance. The implemented formulas are:

Aalen variance Var{F̂k(t)}=∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]2dj(Yj−1)(Yj−dj)+∑tj≤tŜ2(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj2(Yj−1)−2∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]Ŝ(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj(Yj−dj)(Yj−1). \begin{aligned} \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{F}_k(t)\right \} &= \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]^2 \frac{d_j}{(Y_j-1)(Y_j - d_j)} \\[2pt] &\quad + \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}^2(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j^2\,(Y_j-1)} \\[2pt] &\quad - 2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]\, \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)\,(Y_j-1)}. \end{aligned}

Delta method variance Var{F̂k(t)}=∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]2djYj(Yj−dj)+∑tj≤tŜ2(tj−1)djk(Yj−djk)Yj3−2∑tj≤t[F̂k(t)−F̂k(tj)]Ŝ(tj−1)djkYj2. \begin{aligned} \textrm{Var}\!\left\{\hat{F}_k(t)\right \} &= \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]^2 \frac{d_j}{Y_j\,(Y_j - d_j)} \\[2pt] &\quad + \sum_{t_j \le t} \hat{S}^2(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}\,(Y_j - d_{jk})}{Y_j^3} \\[2pt] &\quad - 2 \sum_{t_j \le t} \bigl[\hat{F}_k(t) - \hat{F}_k(t_j)\bigr]\, \hat{S}(t_{j-1}) \frac{d_{jk}}{Y_j^2}. \end{aligned}

Influence-function representation

Set error = "if" to estimate variance from individual influence-function (IF) contributions. Add report.influence.function = TRUE to return the uncorrected empirical contributions. The classical AJ representation below provides background; the next section describes the finite-jump, fixed-weight calculation implemented in cifcurve(). For unweighted AJ estimates, Zhang and Fine (2008) give the asymptotic linear expansion n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}=n−1/2∑i=1nIFik(t)+op(1), n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t) - F_k(t)\} = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n IF_{ik}(t) + o_p(1), The process n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t) - F_k(t)\} also converges weakly to a tight Gaussian process. Let Y(t)Y(t) be the sample at-risk process, and define y(t)=limn→∞n−1Y(t). y(t) = \lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1}Y(t). For continuous cumulative hazards, let Mi(t)M_i(t) and Mik(t)M_{ik}(t) be the martingales for all events and cause-kk events, respectively, for observation ii. The influence function is then IFik(t)=∫0tS(u−)dMik(u)y(u)−∫0tS(u−){∫0u−dMi(v)y(v)}dΛk(u). \begin{aligned} IF_{ik}(t) &= \int_0^t S(u^-) \frac{dM_{ik}(u)}{y(u)} \\ &\quad - \int_0^t S(u^-) \left\{ \int_0^{u^-} \frac{dM_i(v)}{y(v)} \right\} d\Lambda_k(u). \end{aligned} Equivalently, after changing the order of integration, IFik(t)=∫0tS(u−)y(u)dMik(u)−∫0tFk(t)−Fk(u−)y(u)dMi(u). IF_{ik}(t) = \int_0^t \frac{S(u^-)}{y(u)}\,dM_{ik}(u) - \int_0^t \frac{F_k(t)-F_k(u^-)}{y(u)}\,dM_i(u). A consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of n1/2{F̂k(t)−Fk(t)}n^{1/2}\{\hat F_k(t)-F_k(t)\} is 1n∑i=1n{IF̂ik(t)}2, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \{\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)\}^2, so the variance of F̂k(t)\hat F_k(t) itself is estimated by Var̂{F̂k(t)}=1n2∑i=1n{IF̂ik(t)}2. \widehat{\textrm{Var}}\!\left\{\hat F_k(t)\right\} = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \{\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)\}^2.

The preceding representation applies to unweighted AJ estimation under the stated assumptions, including continuous cumulative hazards. By contrast, cifcurve() differentiates the empirical weighted product-limit estimator, allowing tied event times. The C++ routine stores contributions on the estimator scale (conventionally IF̂ik(t)/n\widehat{IF}_{ik}(t)/n); their squared sum estimates the variance of F̂k(t)\hat F_k(t). Externally supplied weights remain fixed, so propensity-score estimation is not included. Deng and Wang (2025) derive influence functions that account for estimating propensity scores.

Fixed-weight IF and Fay–Graubard variances

This section details the calculations behind error = "if" and error = "fay". Both retain the same KM/AJ point estimate but use different contributions to estimate variance. The C++ engine differentiates the finite-jump product limit, with or without weights, within each stratum. Only positive-weight observations enter the variance and degrees-of-freedom calculations; let mm be their number. Without supplied weights, set wi=1w_i=1. Define Yjw=∑iwiYij,ĥjk=∑iwiΔNijkYjw,ĥj=∑kĥjk, Y_j^w=\sum_i w_iY_{ij},\qquad \hat h_{jk}=\frac{\sum_i w_i\Delta N_{ijk}}{Y_j^w},\qquad \hat h_j=\sum_k\hat h_{jk}, where Yij=1(Ti≥tj)Y_{ij}=1(T_i\ge t_j) and ΔNijk=1(Ti=tj,ϵi=k)\Delta N_{ijk}=1(T_i=t_j,\epsilon_i=k). For survival data there is one event cause. Set rijk=wi(ΔNijk−Yijĥjk),rij=∑krijk. r_{ijk}=w_i(\Delta N_{ijk}-Y_{ij}\hat h_{jk}),\qquad r_{ij}=\sum_k r_{ijk}. Starting from ai0S=aik0F=0a^S_{i0}=a^F_{ik0}=0 and Ŝ0=1\hat S_0=1, the uncorrected empirical IF contributions obey aikjF=aik,j−1F+ĥjkai,j−1S+Ŝj−1rijk/Yjw,aijS=(1−ĥj)ai,j−1S−Ŝj−1rij/Yjw. \begin{aligned} a^F_{ikj}&=a^F_{ik,j-1}+\hat h_{jk}a^S_{i,j-1} +\hat S_{j-1}r_{ijk}/Y_j^w,\\ a^S_{ij}&=(1-\hat h_j)a^S_{i,j-1} -\hat S_{j-1}r_{ij}/Y_j^w. \end{aligned} With error = "if", the variance is ∑i(aijS)2\sum_i(a^S_{ij})^2 for KM survival or ∑i(aikjF)2\sum_i(a^F_{ikj})^2 for the cause-kk CIF. The contributions are already on the estimator scale, with the usual 1/n1/n factor incorporated. This recursion differentiates the finite-jump product limit used by the software, rather than relying on a continuous-hazard approximation.

With error = "fay", the Fay–Graubard correction (Fay and Graubard 2001) applies the same recursion after replacing rijkr_{ijk} and rijr_{ij} by HijrijkH_{ij}r_{ijk} and HijrijH_{ij}r_{ij}, respectively, where ℓij=wiYijYjw,Hij={1−min⁡(0.75,ℓij)}−1/2. \ell_{ij}=\frac{w_iY_{ij}}{Y_j^w},\qquad H_{ij}=\{1-\min(0.75,\ell_{ij})\}^{-1/2}. The Fay–Graubard (FG) variance sums the squared corrected contributions; the KM/AJ point estimate is unchanged. The leverage cap is fixed at 0.75 and reported as fay.bound; users cannot set it directly. Both "fg" and "fay-graubard" are aliases for "fay".

Even when error = "fay", report.influence.function = TRUE returns uncorrected contributions for the event probability 1 - fit$surv. Observations with zero weight contribute zero.

Working degrees of freedom for IF-t and FG-t

With conf.dist = "t", cifcurve() uses a time- and stratum-specific t critical value rather than a normal one. For error = "if", df.method selects deletion allocation ("deletion", FDF) or equal allocation ("equal", EDF). For error = "fay", only deletion allocation is available (FG-t). The trace ratio below provides working, not exact finite-sample Student, degrees of freedom.

The calculation starts with individual weighted hazard scores Uhji=wi{Δ𝑵i(tj)−Yij𝒉j}U_{h_j i}=w_i\{\Delta\mathbf N_i(t_j)-Y_{ij}\mathbf h_j\}, stacked over event times tj≤tt_j\le t. Hazard logits use the no-event category as the baseline, except at complete exit, when a positive cause becomes the baseline; only positive-probability coordinates are retained. No additional time- or cause-specific equation multipliers are used. At the fitted parameter ϑ̂\hat\vartheta, define Ωi=−∂Ui∂ϑ⊤,B=∑iΩi,c=∇ϑθ̂(t), \Omega_i=-\frac{\partial U_i}{\partial\vartheta^\top},\qquad B=\sum_i\Omega_i,\qquad c=\nabla_\vartheta\hat\theta(t), where θ̂(t)\hat\theta(t) is the KM survival estimate or the AJ CIF. This production calculation contains hazard scores only, with no propensity-score estimating equations.

Deletion allocation (FDF). The default df.method = "deletion" uses ρi=c⊤{(B−Ωi)−1−B−1}c,αi=ρi/∑jρj. \rho_i=c^\top\{(B-\Omega_i)^{-1}-B^{-1}\}c,\qquad \alpha_i=\rho_i/\sum_j\rho_j. These quantities use derivatives at the original fit; they do not require refitting after deleting each observation. The relevant deleted blocks must be invertible, and the allocation must be nonnegative and nonzero. Because the allocation can depend on how estimating equations are normalized, the score convention above is part of the method definition.

Equal allocation (EDF). For error = "if", df.method = "equal" sets αi=1/m\alpha_i=1/m. In the uncorrected IF calculation, the resulting degrees of freedom are invariant to fixed invertible score transformations when the derivatives are transformed consistently. This holds for a fixed active set, not for arbitrary parameter-dependent transformations. EDF degrees of freedom generally do not equal m−1m-1, and EDF is unavailable with FG-t.

For either allocation, let Hi=IH_i=I for IF-t, and use the diagonal matrix containing the factors HijH_{ij} above for FG-t. Form TiH=HiUi,MH=∑iTiH(TiH)⊤,LijH=c⊤B−1Hi{1(i=j)I−ΩiB−1},QH=LHblockdiag⁡(α1MH,…,αmMH)(LH)⊤,ν̂H(t)={tr⁡(QH)}2tr⁡(QH2). \begin{aligned} T_i^H&=H_iU_i,& M_H&=\sum_iT_i^H(T_i^H)^\top,\\ L^H_{ij}&=c^\top B^{-1}H_i\{1(i=j)I-\Omega_iB^{-1}\},\\ Q_H&=L^H\operatorname{blockdiag}(\alpha_1M_H,\ldots,\alpha_mM_H)(L^H)^\top,\\ \hat\nu_H(t)&=\frac{\{\operatorname{tr}(Q_H)\}^2}{\operatorname{tr}(Q_H^2)}. \end{aligned} Here LHL^H has blocks LijHL^H_{ij}. FG-t uses the original, uncorrected derivatives B,ΩiB,\Omega_i and deletion allocation; it does not differentiate HiH_i. The correction enters MHM_H and LHL^H at the indicated positions. Thus IF-t (deletion) and FG-t can differ in both variance and degrees of freedom.

The trace ratio matches moments of a Gaussian working quadratic form, following the Satterthwaite principle. It does not imply an exact t distribution or guarantee improved small-sample coverage. FDF uses Fay-type deletion allocation; EDF uses equal allocation. Even with the same IF variance, different allocations may produce different critical values.

Confidence interval options

Method combinations

The following argument combinations select the available IF/FG interval methods. Setting conf.dist = "t" without error selects IF, even for unweighted data. df.method affects IF-t, but not normal-reference intervals.

Construction error conf.dist df.method
IF-normal "if" "normal" Not used
IF-t (FDF) "if" "t" "deletion" (default)
IF-t (EDF) "if" "t" "equal"
FG-normal "fay" "normal" Not used
FG-t "fay" "t" "deletion"

Student intervals require error = "if" or "fay" and the C++ engine (engine = "calculateAJ_Rcpp", the default, or "auto"). The legacy "calculateKM" engine does not support them. Degrees of freedom are calculated separately for each time and stratum and may be costly for large risk sets.

Transformations and probability scale

The transformation is applied to the stored probability: p=Ŝ(t)p=\hat S(t) for KM, but p=1−F̂1(t)p=1-\hat F_1(t) for AJ (fit$surv). At an interior estimate with positive variance, the transformed limits are obtained from g(p)±q|g′(p)|SÊ(p),q={z(1+conf.int)/2,normal,tν̂(t),(1+conf.int)/2,Student. g(p)\ \pm\ q\,|g'(p)|\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(p),\qquad q=\begin{cases} z_{(1+\mathrm{conf.int})/2},&\text{normal},\\ t_{\hat\nu(t),(1+\mathrm{conf.int})/2},&\text{Student}. \end{cases} The limits are mapped back through g−1g^{-1} and ordered on the probability scale. Where needed, they are restricted to the transformation’s range before inversion and to [0,1][0,1] afterward. The supported transformations are:

conf.type g(p)g(p)
"plain" pp
"log" log⁡p\log p
"log-log" log⁡(−log⁡p)\log(-\log p)
"logit" log⁡{p/(1−p)}\log\{p/(1-p)\}
"arcsin" (default; aliases "arcsine-square root", "a") arcsin⁡p\arcsin\sqrt p

The default is the arcsine–square-root CI transformation. This option is distinct from type.y, which controls the vertical plotting scale.

For AJ, fit$lower and fit$upper are limits for 1−F̂1(t)1-\hat F_1(t), so the CIF limits are 1 - fit$upper and 1 - fit$lower. Accordingly, "log-log" applies log⁡[−log⁡{1−F̂1(t)}]\log[-\log\{1-\hat F_1(t)\}], not log⁡[−log⁡F̂1(t)]\log[-\log\hat F_1(t)]. When displaying risk, cifplot() uses the CIF limits. conf.type = "none" (or "n") omits intervals. By default, std.err is on the probability scale; report.survfit.std.err = TRUE instead uses the log scale of the stored surv component.

Boundaries, failures, and one-sided tests

For the C++ IF/FG calculations, a valid estimate of 0 or 1 receives a singleton interval. This is a boundary convention, not a coverage guarantee. Limits are missing for interior estimates with zero or invalid variance, unavailable Student degrees of freedom, or times beyond positive-weight follow-up. A failed Student interval does not fall back to a normal interval. The fit records df, df.reason, critical.value, and conf.status by time and stratum; summary(fit, times = ..., extend = TRUE) preserves these diagnostics, including missing limits outside follow-up support.

These intervals are pointwise, not simultaneous confidence bands. The optional one-sided fixed-time probability test using time.point and null.hypothesis retains a normal reference even when conf.dist = "t" is selected for intervals. Its default alternative is higher survival for KM and lower event-1 cumulative incidence for AJ.

Worked examples

These short examples demonstrate cifcurve() options rather than a full analysis workflow. With this small synthetic dataset, working degrees of freedom or CIs may be unavailable at some times; conf.status indicates why. For complete analyses and tables, see Worked examples and Reporting results.

library(cifmodeling)
example_data <- data.frame(
  time = 1:12,
  status = c(1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0),
  weight = c(1, 1.5, 0.8, 1.2, 1, 0.7, 1.3, 1, 0.9, 1.1, 1, 1)
)

# AJ with IF-t and equal-allocation degrees of freedom.
fit_edf <- cifcurve(
  Event(time, status) ~ 1, data = example_data, weights = "weight",
  outcome.type = "competing-risk", error = "if",
  conf.dist = "t", df.method = "equal", conf.type = "log-log"
)
at_five <- summary(fit_edf, times = 5)
data.frame(
  time = at_five$time, CIF = 1 - at_five$surv,
  SE = at_five$std.err, lower = 1 - at_five$upper,
  upper = 1 - at_five$lower, df = at_five$df,
  critical.value = at_five$critical.value,
  df.reason = at_five$df.reason,
  status = at_five$conf.status
)
##   time    CIF        SE      lower     upper       df critical.value df.reason
## 1    5 0.1904 0.1220426 0.04291352 0.6383596 10.94327       2.202378        ok
##   status
## 1     ok
# KM for the composite of either event, with FG-t.
example_data$composite_event <- as.integer(example_data$status > 0)
fit_fg <- cifcurve(
  Event(time, composite_event) ~ 1, data = example_data,
  outcome.type = "survival", error = "fay",
  conf.dist = "t", conf.type = "arcsin"
)

The first output table shows the event-1 CIF and its CI on the probability scale, along with degrees of freedom, the critical value, and inference status. The same diagnostics are stored as fit_edf$df, fit_edf$df.reason, fit_edf$critical.value, and fit_edf$conf.status on the original event-time grid; use summary(fit_edf, times = ...) to extract them at a chosen time. In the second fit, error = "fay" changes the variance, while conf.dist = "t" changes the reference critical value.

To plot Student intervals, first fit them with cifcurve() and pass the result to cifplot(). The cifplot() formula interface does not forward conf.dist or df.method to cifcurve().

cifplot(fit_edf, outcome.type = "competing-risk", add.risktable = FALSE)

See Function reference for the full set of arguments and Reporting cumulative incidence for extracting estimates and building tables.
